title: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed
hook: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat, the pillar about money. Your line was what you give purifies what you keep. What did you give away, and how did the rest feel? Day twenty.

Think of the person you'd hand your house keys to without a second thought. Not the most impressive person you know. The most trustworthy. Maybe you couldn't even say why; they've just never once let you down. Now picture a whole city that felt that way about one man. People who argued about everything, clans who'd fight over a camel, all agreed on him. They gave him a nickname for it. And years later, many of those same people refused to believe what he told them, and still kept leaving their valuables in his care. Today: the man at the center of it all, told the way Islam tells him. In words only.
screen: `WHO GETS YOUR HOUSE KEYS?` → `A WHOLE CITY TRUSTED ONE MAN.` → `TRUSTED, NOT YET BELIEVED.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, peace be upon him. Muslims never draw or picture him; he's known through words, so words are all we'll use. He was born in Mecca, around the year 570. His father died before he was born. His mother died when he was six. His grandfather took him in, and died two years later. His uncle Abu Talib raised him after that. So when the Qur'an speaks to him later, it can say, in Pickthall's words: “Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?” He grew up herding sheep, then traveled with the trade caravans. A wealthy widow and merchant named Khadijah hired him to lead hers, and was so struck by his honesty that she proposed marriage. By then Mecca had a name for him: al-Amin, the trustworthy. The early biographies tell a story about it. The clans were rebuilding the Ka'ba, and they nearly came to blows over who would get the honor of setting the sacred Black Stone back in its place. They agreed to let the next man through the gate decide. It was him. He spread out a cloak, set the stone on it, and had a man from each clan lift a corner, together. Then he set it in place himself. At forty, he began to receive the Qur'an. And a hadith in Bukhari tells how he stood on a hill and asked his people: if I told you an army was behind this hill, would you believe me? They said: we've never known you to lie. Then he told them his message, and many turned away. Trusted first. Believed, by many, only later.
screen: `AN ORPHAN IN MECCA.` · `A MERCHANT, AND KHADIJAH.` · `AL-AMIN — AND THE BLACK STONE.` · `WE'VE NEVER KNOWN YOU TO LIE.` · then, large: `AL-AMIN — THE TRUSTWORTHY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think of someone who trusts you with something. A secret, a key, a child, a password, a job. Picture them handing it over. Notice what it feels like to be trusted. Then think of one small promise you've made lately and haven't kept yet. Nothing dramatic. A call, a book to return, a message you said you'd send. Just hold it. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it. The bell holds the time.
The Prophet, peace be upon him. An orphan, a shepherd, a merchant, called al-Amin, the trustworthy, long before most believed him. Twentieth word.
Your line: al-Amin, the trustworthy. Today, keep that one small promise you were holding. Do it quietly, before anyone reminds you. Day twenty.

howItsDone: Muslims say "peace be upon him" (or write ﷺ) after the Prophet's name, never picture him, and learn his life, the sira, from the Qur'an, the hadith and the early biographies.

original.note: Arabic: the trustworthy, the Prophet's name in Mecca before his prophethood, from the root of amana, trust.

trapdoor: what you thought: the founder of a religion.
what it means: the Prophet ﷺ — for Muslims the last messenger of God; an orphan and merchant whom Mecca called al-Amin before he received the Qur'an.
what a scholar hears: the Qur'an itself recalls his orphanhood (93:6); the Black Stone story comes from the early biography of Ibn Ishaq; and al-Amin shares a root with amana, trust, and iman, faith.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (as edited by Ibn Hisham): early life, Khadijah, the Black Stone
Sahih al-Bukhari 4770 (the call from Mount Safa)

notes: Dates and ages from the traditional sira: born c. 570 (the Year of the Elephant); mother Amina died when he was six; grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib when he was eight; first revelation at forty. Confirm.
Khadijah proposing marriage and the Black Stone arbitration are from Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham (paraphrased). The 'next man through the gate' detail is as commonly retold; confirm.

Opponents continuing to leave deposits with him (the hook's 'still kept leaving their valuables in his care') refers to the sira's account that 'Ali stayed behind at the hijra to return them. Confirm.
Bukhari 4770 (Safa): paraphrased; 'an army behind this hill' (literally horsemen in the valley). Confirm.
The index word is 'the Prophet ﷺ' with the honorific; kept exactly. The script says 'peace be upon him' at first mention and states that he is never depicted.
Original: al-Amin rather than 'Muhammad' because the carry teaches it. Root '-m-n shared with amana and iman; confirm.
